context_blurb:
A vaccine trains the body to know a germ before the real one arrives. That immunology is settled, and it helped end smallpox. Vaccines are also made by companies and overseen by governments, and that record has been examined in hearings, courts and studies.

A vaccine may hold a killed germ, a weakened living one or a single protein from its surface. Each carries antigens, molecular shapes that the immune system's own cells can learn to recognise. B cells that fit an antigen multiply, and many become plasma cells making antibodies against that one germ. A first dose is slow, and its antibody fades over months. Some cells from the first dose stay on as memory B cells; at a booster they quickly turn into plasma cells, so the response comes within days and is far larger.

In 1774 the Dorset farmer Benjamin Jesty scratched cowpox into his wife's and sons' arms, but he never made his case public. In 1796 the country doctor Edward Jenner gave cowpox to James Phipps, then tested the boy with smallpox matter, and no disease followed. He tested others the same way and published 23 cases in 1798.

In eastern Nigeria late in 1966, the American doctor William Foege had too little vaccine for the mass campaign officials thought necessary. Guided by missionaries' radio reports, his teams vaccinated the people around each case, then the places it was likely to reach next along family and market routes. The outbreak ended within four weeks, and this ring vaccination became the worldwide campaign's method. Smallpox could be ended for good because no animal carried the virus, only people, so once no one was infected it had nowhere left to live. In 1980 it became the only human disease ever declared eradicated.

In 1955 some Cutter Laboratories lots of Salk's killed-virus polio vaccine held live virus, though they had passed their safety tests; by Paul Offit's count, about 200 children were left partly paralysed and 10 died. A congressional hearing that June laid most of the blame on too little checking by the federal Laboratory of Biologics Control, part of the National Institutes of Health. The institutes' director had set aside Bernice Eddy's 1954 report of paralysed test monkeys.

Lawsuits over the DTP shot rose from nine around 1980 to over 200 by the mid-decade, and by late 1985 only one American firm still made pertussis vaccine. The law Congress passed in 1986 made a trade: makers faced far fewer lawsuits, and families could be paid without proving that anyone was at fault. Makers stay liable for faulty manufacture or poor warnings, and a tax on each dose has funded about 5.4 billion dollars in awards.

Since 1990 the CDC and the FDA have run VAERS, which takes reports from anyone, a parent or a vaccine's maker, without first judging them. One report shows only that a problem came after the shot, and after is not because: a rash after a shot might come from a virus, a food or anything else. In 1999 fifteen reports flagged a real risk from a new vaccine, RotaShield. Yet a 2010 report from Ross Lazarus's Harvard Pilgrim Health Care project said vaccine side effects are common but underreported, with fewer than 1 in 100 reported. That figure was the project's reason for its work, not a count it made.

By 2013 the US schedule had grown from seven diseases in the early 1980s to fourteen germs. That year an Institute of Medicine committee saw no significant evidence that following it is unsafe, and credited vaccines for the decline of the diseases they prevent. But it reported that the schedule as a whole, the number, timing and order of its shots, had not been systematically studied, though each vaccine was tested before licensing and watched afterward.

In May 2025 the health department under Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who wants "gold standard science", said new vaccines would need safety trials against a placebo, a dummy shot, before approval. Steven Black, who helped lead Prevnar's baby-vaccine trial in the 1990s, said ethics ruled out a dummy shot there. Its comparison babies got a vaccine against a different disease, an experimental meningococcal shot that Black said gave them a possible benefit. Christine Stabell Benn and Martin Kulldorff argued in 2025 that few vaccines have had a double-blind placebo trial, medicine's gold standard, and proposed such trials for vaccines in use; Paul Offit called them unethical. Any trial needs the parents' informed consent.
